Individual claim severities are strictly positive and strongly right-skewed on the raw scale, with a roughly symmetric shape after taking logs. Choose the matching continuous family. As a light numeric check, if $\ln(X) \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu = 6, \sigma = 1)$, compute the median of $X$.
continuous support on $(0, \infty)$
$\mathrm{Normal}(\mu = 6, \sigma = 1)$

If $\ln(X)$ is $\mathrm{Normal}(\mu, \sigma)$, the median of $X$ is $e^{\mu}$ because the Normal median equals $\mu$. The numeric check illustrates the chosen family; family selection remains the LO hinge.
$\mathrm{median}(X) = e^{6} \approx 403.43$
$\mathrm{median}(X) \approx 403.43$

Choose Lognormal for positive right-skewed severities that are Normal on the log scale; with $\ln(X) \sim \mathrm{Normal}(6, 1)$, $\mathrm{median}(X) = e^{6} \approx 403.43$. Refuse Normal-by-default on the raw severity scale.

For annual mileage versus claim severity, severity is skewed with outliers and the scatter looks roughly increasing but nonlinear. Software reports Pearson $r = 0.25$ and Spearman $\rho = 0.52$. Which correlation measure should you prefer for describing the association, and what must you still refuse?
Spearman $\rho$
Compare $|r|$ and $|\rho|$ in light of the scatter.
$|\rho| = 0.52 > |r| = 0.25$; rank measure captures monotone association better here
Report Spearman $\rho = 0.52$ as the preferred description
Association $\neq$ causation (even if $|\rho|$ is large)
Prefer Spearman $\rho = 0.52$ (monotone, skewed, outlier-prone) over Pearson $r = 0.25$. A large coefficient still does not prove causation.
Defaulting to Pearson because it is the familiar default, or treating Spearman $\rho = 0.52$ as proof that higher mileage causes higher claim severity.

Exponential(rate $\lambda = 0.5$), $U = 0.2$
smallest y with $F(y) \geq U$
CMP closed. Invert the Exponential CDF for (a); find the smallest support point with $F(y) \geq U$ for (b).
Solve F(x) = U for x when F(x) = 1 - e^{-λx}.
For Exponential rate $\lambda$, $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$, so $x = -\ln(1-U)/\lambda$.
$X \approx 0.4463$

$F(1) = 0.3 < 0.55$, so $y = 1$ is too small. $F(2) = 0.8 \geq 0.55$, so the inverse-transform draw is $Y = 2$.
$0.3 < 0.55 \leq 0.8 \Rightarrow Y = 2$

$X \approx 0.4463$ from Exponential(rate 0.5) with $U = 0.2$; $Y = 2$ from the discrete CDF with $U = 0.55$. A black-box RNG call without Uniform-to-inverse-CDF construction is not the inverse transform method.

Claims arrive as a homogeneous Poisson process with rate $\lambda = 1.5$ claims per day. For a 4-day window, name the distribution of the claim count $N(4)$, compute $P(N(4) = 0)$, and state the distribution of the waiting time until the next claim.
$\lambda$
CMP closed. Link process $\mathrm{rate} \times \mathrm{time}$ to the Poisson count mean, then name the interarrival family.
State $N(t)$ for a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$.
In a homogeneous Poisson process with rate $\lambda$, the count in an interval of length t is Poisson with mean $\lambda t$.
$N(4) \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda t = 1.5 \times 4 = 6)$
Compute $P(N(4) = 0)$
Evaluate e^{-6}.
For Poisson(6), $P(N = 0) = e^{-6}$.
Interarrival waiting times are Exponential with the same rate $\lambda = 1.5$. The Poisson count and the Exponential wait are linked but not the same object.
$N(4) \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(6)$ with $P(N(4) = 0) \approx 0.0025$; waiting time until the next claim is Exponential(rate 1.5). Refuse collapsing the count and the wait into one label.
Probability: find $P(X <= 2)$ for X ~ Exp(lambda). Quantile: find x such that $P(X <= x)$ = 0.95. Method class: calculation, tables, or software CDF/quantile functions as appropriate.

Use $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/\theta}$ with $\theta = 250$ and $x = 100$.

For Exponential mean $\theta$, $P(X \leq x) = 1 - e^{-x/\theta}$. Here $x/\theta = 100/250 = 0.4$, so $P(X \leq 100) = 1 - e^{-0.4} \approx 0.3297$. Naming the Exponential family alone does not produce this probability.
Reporting $e^{-0.4} \approx 0.6703$ (the survival probability) instead of $1 - e^{-0.4}$, or treating $\theta = 250$ as a rate so that $F(100) = 1 - e^{-25000}$.
Uses the Exponential CDF with mean θ, not the survival function alone.

$Exponential(mean \theta = 250)$

$median \approx 173.29$

$E[g]$=sum or integral of g times joint; Cov=$E[XY]$-EX EY; Corr=Cov/(SDX SDY).
$E[g(X,Y)]$ is the sum or integral of g(x,y) weighted by the joint distribution. $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]$-$E[X] E[Y]$, and $\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$/(SD(X)SD(Y)).
$E[g(X,Y)]$ is found from marginal means alone for every g, so the joint distribution is unnecessary.
Closed-book. $P(0,0)$=0.2, $P(0,1)$=0.3, $P(1,0)$=0.1, $P(1,1)$=0.4. Compute $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. Enter the numeric value.
Compute $E[X]$, $E[Y]$, $E[XY]$, and covariance.
Only cell (1,1) contributes to $E[XY]$. Then centre: $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]$.
Enter the covariance value, not $E[XY]$ alone.
Only cell (1,1) contributes to $E[XY]$. Subtracting the product of the means gives 0.05: $E[X]=0.5$, $E[Y]=0.7$, $E[XY]=0.4$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.4-(0.5)(0.7)=0.05$.
Assuming independence from marginals or using $E[XY]$ as covariance without centring.
Uses $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]$, not the uncentred product alone.

Two binary indicators (X, Y) for a household have joint PMF $P(0,0)$ = 0.30, $P(0,1)$ = 0.20, $P(1,0)$ = 0.20, $P(1,1)$ = 0.30, where X = 1 if a contents claim occurs and Y = 1 if a buildings claim occurs. Compute $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$, $\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y)$, and $E[X + 2Y]$.
CMP closed. Form $E[X]$, $E[Y]$, and $E[XY]$ first, then Cov, then Corr, then $E[X+2Y]$ by linearity.
Find $E[X]$, $E[Y]$, and $E[XY]$ from the joint table.
For binary indicators, $E[X] = P(X = 1)$ and $E[Y] = P(Y = 1)$. The product moment is $E[XY] = P(X = 1, Y = 1)$.
Use Cov = $E[XY] − E[X] E[Y]$ and divide by $\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$.
Covariance subtracts the product of means from $E[XY]$. Each margin is Bernoulli(0.5), so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{Var}(Y)$ = 0.25 and $\sigma_{X} = \sigma_{Y} = 0.5$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0.05$; $\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y) = 0.20$
Evaluate $E[X + 2Y]$ and refuse Corr=0⇒independence
Apply linearity, then state why $\operatorname{Corr} \neq 0$ here does not finish an independence claim.
Linearity gives $E[X + 2Y] = E[X]$ + 2$E[Y]$ without needing the joint again. Correlation here is 0.20, not zero; even Corr = 0 would not by itself prove independence for general joint distributions.
$E[X + 2Y] = 1.50$; $\operatorname{Corr} \neq 0$ here (and $\operatorname{Corr} = 0 \neq$ independence in general)
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0.05$; $\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y) = 0.20$; $E[X + 2Y] = 1.50. Zero correlation is not automatic independence, and here correlation is not zero.$
Computing Cov as $E[XY]$ alone (forgetting to subtract $E[X] E[Y]$), or claiming that Corr = 0 would prove independence for any joint distribution.

A household book records indicators (X, Y) with joint PMF $P(0,0)$ = 0.50, $P(0,1)$ = 0.10, $P(1,0)$ = 0.20, $P(1,1)$ = 0.20, where X = 1 if a theft claim occurs and Y = 1 if a fire claim occurs in the same year. Compute the marginals, check whether X and Y are independent, and refuse equating zero covariance with independence in general.
Sum rows/columns for $P(X)$ and $P(Y)$.
Compare $P(0,0)$ with $P(X=0)P(Y=0)$, and at least one other cell.
Independence requires $P(x,y) = P(X=x)P(Y=y)$ for every cell. Here $P(X=0)P(Y=0) = 0.60\times 0.70 = 0.42$, but $P(0,0) = 0.50 \neq 0.42$, so $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.
$0.60\times 0.70 = 0.42 \neq 0.50 = P(0,0)$ $\rightarrow$ not independent

Marginals are $P(X=0)=0.60$, $P(X=1)=0.40$, $P(Y=0)=0.70$, $P(Y=1)=0.30$. Since $0.60\times 0.70 = 0.42 \neq P(0,0) = 0.50$, $X$ and $Y$ are not independent. Zero covariance would not by itself prove independence in general.
Declaring independence from a quick look at the table, or treating $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$ as a general proof of independence without checking joint factorisation.
Today I will force the candidate through $E[aX+bY]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)$ with an explicit dependence note. Refuse ignoring Cov and refuse Chapter-2-complete claims.
$E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y]$ → $\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$ → refuse dropping Cov when dependent.
Yesterday you placed Cov/Corr and $E[g(X,Y)]$ (2.2.3). Today applies linear combination mean and variance.
Closed-book, state $E[aX+bY]$ in terms of $E[X]$, $E[Y]$.
State $\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)$ including the covariance term when needed.
$E=aE[X]+bE[Y]$; $\operatorname{Var}=a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}$.
$E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y]$, and $\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$.
$\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)$=a$\operatorname{Var}(X)$+b$\operatorname{Var}(Y)$+2ab$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$, because variance is linear in constants.
$\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ for all $X$ and $Y$, because covariance never affects a linear combination.
$E[aX+bY]=a^{2}E[X]+b^{2}E[Y]$, matching the squared coefficients used in variance.
Closed-book. $\operatorname{Var}(X)$=4, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$=9, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$=2. Compute $\operatorname{Var}(2X-Y)$. Enter the numeric value.
Expand $a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(X)+b^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$ with $a=2$ and $b=-1$.
The cross-term $2ab\operatorname{Cov}$ is negative here because $b=-1$.
With a=2 and b=-1, the cross-term is negative: 2abCov=-8. So $\operatorname{Var}(2X-Y)=2^{2}(4)+(-1)^{2}(9)+2(2)(-1)(2)=16+9-8=17$.
Retains the signed covariance cross-term in $\operatorname{Var}(2X-Y)$.
Mean and variance of $2X - Y$ with nonzero covariance

Portfolio losses $X$ and $Y$ (£000) satisfy $E[X] = 10$, $E[Y] = 4$, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 9$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 4$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 3$. For the linear combination $L = 2X - Y$, compute $E[L]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(L)$.
$\operatorname{Var}(X)$
$\operatorname{Var}(Y)$
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$
CMP closed. Apply linearity for the mean, then expand $\operatorname{Var}(2X - Y)$ including the covariance term.
Compute $E[2X - Y]$
Use $E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]$ with $a = 2$, $b = -1$.
Expand $\operatorname{Var}(2X - Y)$
Write $a^{2}\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y) + 2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$.
Variance of a linear combination needs the covariance whenever dependence is present. Here $a = 2$ and $b = -1$, so $2ab\operatorname{Cov} = 2(2)(-1)(3) = -12$.
$\operatorname{Var}(L) = 4\times 9 + 1\times 4 + 2(2)(-1)(3) = 36 + 4 - 12 = 28$
$\operatorname{Var}(L) = 28$
Dropping the covariance term as if $X$ and $Y$ were uncorrelated gives $36 + 4 = 40$, which overstates $\operatorname{Var}(L)$ when $\operatorname{Cov} = 3 > 0$ and the combination is $2X - Y$.
$E[2X - Y] = 16$; $\operatorname{Var}(2X - Y) = 28. Omitting \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 3 incorrectly yields 40.$
Computing $\operatorname{Var}(2X - Y)$ as 4$\operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y)$ = 40 and dropping the covariance term even though $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ = 3 is given.
Closed-book. Joint PMF: $P(0,0)$=0.10, $P(0,1)$=0.20, $P(1,0)$=0.30, $P(1,1)$=0.40. Compute $P(Y=1|X=1)$. Enter the value as a decimal (not a fraction).
Sum the X=1 row for the marginal $P(X=1)=0.30+0.40$, then divide the (1,1) cell by that row total.
Sum the X=1 row for the marginal, then divide the (1,1) cell by that row total. $P(X=1)=0.70$ and $P(Y=1|X=1)=0.40/0.70\approx 0.571$.
Forms $P(Y=1|X=1)$ from the normalised $X=1$ slice, not from a raw joint cell.

A property book records indicators (X, Y) with joint PMF $P(0,0)$ = 0.55, $P(0,1)$ = 0.15, $P(1,0)$ = 0.20, $P(1,1)$ = 0.10, where X = 1 if a flood claim occurs and Y = 1 if a wind claim occurs in the same year. Compute $P(Y = 1)$ and $P(X = 1 | Y = 1)$.
Form the marginal $P(Y = 1)$
The marginal for Y = 1 sums over X: $P(Y = 1) = P(0,1)$ + $P(1,1)$.
Form the conditional $P(X = 1 | Y = 1)$
Divide $P(1,1)$ by $P(Y = 1)$.
State why $P(1,1)$ = 0.10 is not $P(Y = 1)$.
Joint cell $\neq$ marginal or conditional
$P(Y = 1) = 0.25$; $P(X = 1 \mid Y = 1) = 0.40$. The joint table is not interchangeable with its margins or conditionals without these moves.
Reporting $P(Y = 1)$ = 0.10 because that is the flood-and-wind cell, or taking $P(X = 1 | Y = 1)$ = 0.10 without dividing by the marginal 0.25.

Expected Y under Y|X=x; a function of x and generally different from $E[Y]$.
$E[Y|X=x]$ is the expected value of Y under the conditional distribution of Y given X=x. As x varies it is a function of x, and it need not equal $E[Y]$.
$E[Y|X=x]$ is always the unconditional mean $E[Y]$ because expectation removes all conditioning information.
$E[Y|X=x]$ is the joint probability $P(X=x,Y=y)$ evaluated at the largest y.

Normalise the $X=1$ row by $P(X=1)=0.30+0.40$, then average Y under that conditional distribution.
Normalise the X=1 row, then average Y under that conditional distribution. Given $X=1$, $P(Y=1|X=1)=0.40/0.70\approx 0.571$, so $E[Y|X=1]=0(0.30/0.70)+1(0.40/0.70)\approx 0.571$.

$E[Y] \neq E[Y|X]$ as objects

$\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(E[Y|X])$ only, because conditional variation disappears after conditioning.

Stopping at $E[Y|X]$ or averaging conditional means without probability weights.

A risk type indicator X equals 0 with probability 0.4 and 1 with probability 0.6. Conditional on X, claim cost Y (£00) satisfies $E[Y | X = 0]$ = 5, $E[Y | X = 1]$ = 12, $\operatorname{Var}(Y | X = 0)$ = 4, and $\operatorname{Var}(Y | X = 1)$ = 9. Compute $E[Y]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ using the conditioning formulae.
$\operatorname{Var}(Y | X)$
CMP closed. Apply $E[Y] = E[E[Y|X]]$, then $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = E[\operatorname{Var}(Y|X)] + \operatorname{Var}(E[Y|X])$.
Average the conditional means with $P(X)$.

$MSE_{1}=\frac{2}{n}$; $MSE_{2}=\frac{0.75}{n}$; prefer $\hat{\theta}_{2}$. Definitions alone are not a comparison.
Dropping the $\mathrm{bias}^{2}$ term, preferring unbiasedness over MSE, or mishandling $(\frac{0.5}{\sqrt{n}})^{2}$.

$MSE_{1}=\frac{2}{n}$ and $MSE_{2}=(\frac{0.5}{\sqrt{n}})^{2}$ + $\frac{0.5}{n} = \frac{0.75}{n}$. Prefer $\hat{\theta}_{2}$ on MSE. Naming the definitions of bias and MSE is not itself a comparison of these two estimators.

$MSE_{1}=\frac{2}{n}$ and $MSE_{2}=\frac{0.25}{n}$ + $\frac{0.5}{n} = \frac{0.75}{n}$, but prefer $\hat{\theta}_{1}$ because any unbiased estimator beats any biased one on MSE.

Bias is $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta})$. MSE equals the absolute bias, and consistency means the estimator is unbiased for every finite n.

Closed-book. Estimator A is unbiased with $\operatorname{Var}(A)$=4/n. Estimator B has $\operatorname{Bias}(B)$=1/n and $\operatorname{Var}(B)$=1/n. Which statement is correct?

Independent samples from portfolios A and B (Normal, known variances): $n_{A} = 40$, $\bar{x}_{A}$ = £8,200, $\sigma_{A}$ = £1,200; $n_{B} = 45$, $\bar{x}_{B}$ = £7,600, $\sigma_{B}$ = £1,100. Construct a 95% CI for $\mu_{A} - \mu_{B}$.
$n_A, \bar{x}_A, \sigma_A$
$n_B, \bar{x}_B, \sigma_B$
CMP closed. Write $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\sigma_{A}^{2}/n_{A} + \sigma_{B}^{2}/n_{B}}$ before the interval.
Compute $\bar{x}_{A} - \bar{x}_{B}$.
The natural centre for $\mu_{A} - \mu_{B}$ is the difference of sample means.
$\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B = 600$
$SE \approx 250.777$
Compute $600 \pm 1.96 \times 250.777$.
95% CI for $\mu_{A} - \mu_{B}$: approximately (£108.48, £1,091.52).
Pooling into $\sqrt{\sigma^{2}(1/n_{A}+1/n_{B})}$ with a single $\sigma$, or subtracting SEs instead of adding variances under the square root.
Closed-book. From a large sample you obtain a 95% CI for mean claim size $\mu$ as $(120, 140)$. Which statement is correct?

Frequentist coverage is about the procedure and the parameter μ, not about the next observation. Treating μ as a random draw inside the interval, or equating narrowness with certainty, misstates coverage.
95% coverage for $\mu$ under repeated sampling; not a prediction interval for the next claim.
The interval comes from a procedure that covers the unknown parameter $\mu$ in 95% of repeated samples. It is not a claim that the next claim amount falls between 120 and 140 with probability 95%.
$\mu$ is a random variable that equals 130 with probability 95%, and the interval endpoints are fixed constants only.

A random sample of $n = 36$ commercial property claims has sample mean $\bar{x}$ = £12,000. Claim sizes are modelled as Normal with known $\sigma$ = £1,800. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$.
$\bar{x}$
$\sigma$
CMP closed. Write the z-interval formula $\bar{x} \pm z_{0.975}\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ before substituting.

For a Normal mean with known $\sigma$, $\operatorname{SE}(\bar{x}) = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$.
Compute $12000 \pm 588$.
Centre at $\bar{x}$ and add/subtract the half-width.
Using $\sigma$ instead of $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ in the margin ($1.96 \times 1800$) and producing a wildly wide interval, or using $\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{36}$ incorrectly as 36.
Closed-book. You fit a model to historical annual losses and need an interval for next year's loss $Y_{\mathrm{new}}$. Which statement is correct?
Prediction targets $Y_{\mathrm{new}}$; a CI for $E[Y]$ targets the mean. Proper prediction intervals account for both parameter uncertainty and process variation.
Prediction interval covers $Y_{\mathrm{new}}$; a CI for $E[Y]$ does not substitute.

A prediction interval aims to cover the future observation $Y_{\mathrm{new}}$ (parameter uncertainty plus process/residual variation). A confidence interval for $E[Y]$ covers only that mean parameter and does not finish the prediction-interval task.
A confidence interval for mean loss already covers $Y_{\mathrm{new}}$ with the same coverage probability, so no separate prediction interval is needed.
A prediction interval covers $E[Y]$ only; covering $Y_{\mathrm{new}}$ would require a parameter confidence interval instead.
From n = 25 independent Normal claims with known $\sigma$ = £40, the sample mean is $\bar{x}$ = £500. Construct a 95% prediction interval for one future independent claim Y.
$\bar{x}$
$\sigma$
CMP closed. Write the prediction SE $\sigma\sqrt{1 + 1/n}$ before the interval.
Compute $\sigma\sqrt{1 + 1/n}$.
A future observation has variance $\sigma^{2}$ plus the variance of $\bar{x}$, so the prediction SE is $\sigma\sqrt{1 + 1/n}$, not $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.
$SE_pred \approx 40.792$
$half-width \approx 79.953$
Compute $500 \pm 79.953$.
Centre at $\bar{x}$; the wider SE distinguishes prediction from mean estimation.
Using the mean CI half-width $1.96 \times 40/\sqrt{25} = 15.68$ instead of the prediction form $1.96 \times 40\sqrt{1+1/25} \approx 79.95$.
Paired data should be analysed with the independent two-sample test whenever $n_{1} = n_{2}$.
z-test for one Normal mean ($\sigma$ known); two-sample proportion test; paired test on differences; permutation $\neq$ basic parametric.

(a) one Normal mean with $\sigma$ known → one-sample Normal/z-test; (b) two independent binomial proportions → two-sample proportion test with Normal approximation; (c) paired Normal differences → paired test on differences. Permutation tests are a different approach, not a substitute for these basic parametric tests.

Test $H_{0}\colon \mu$ = £500 vs $H_{1}\colon \mu \neq$ £500 for mean repair cost. A sample of $n = 36$ repairs has $\bar{x}$ = £520. Assume Normal data with known $\sigma$ = £60. Compute the $z$ statistic and the two-sided $p$-value using $\Phi(2.0) = 0.9772$. Decide at $\alpha = 0.05$.
$n, \bar{x}, \sigma$
$\alpha$
CMP closed. Write $z = (\bar{x} - \mu_{0})/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$ before looking up the $p$-value.
Compute $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ and then z.
One-sample z-test standardises the sample mean under $H_{0}$.
Compute $2\bigl[1 - \Phi(2)\bigr]$.
Reject $H_{0}$ when $p \leq \alpha$.
$0.0456 < 0.05 \Rightarrow reject H_{0}$
Reject $H_{0}$ at 5%.
Using $(\bar{x} - \mu_{0})/\sigma = 20/60 \approx 0.33$ instead of dividing by $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 10$, which collapses the test statistic toward zero.
Closed-book. You test whether claim counts follow a Poisson distribution; $\lambda$ is estimated from the same sample. Which statement is correct?
Fit Poisson probabilities with $\hat{\lambda}$, form expected counts, and reduce DF by one for $\hat{\lambda}$. Independence testing is not GOF to a named distribution.
$E = n \times$ Poisson probabilities at $\hat{\lambda}$; DF = bins - 1 - 1; independence $\neq$ GOF.
Forgetting the DF reduction for $\hat{\lambda}$, or treating independence as GOF.

Expected frequencies are $n$ times fitted Poisson probabilities using $\hat{\lambda}$. Degrees of freedom are (number of bins - 1 - number of estimated parameters), so subtract 1 for $\hat{\lambda}$. A chi-square test of independence in a two-way table is a different procedure.
Expected frequencies use $\hat{\lambda}$, but degrees of freedom stay at (bins - 1) with no reduction for estimating $\lambda$.
Because $\lambda$ is estimated, replace GOF by a two-way independence test on a contingency table of counts.
Expected frequencies are n/$\hat{\lambda}$ in every bin, regardless of the Poisson probabilities for those bins.

common expected count under H₀
$5 - 1$ categories
CMP closed. Write $\chi^{2} = \sum (O_{i}-E_{i})^{2}/E_{i}$ before summing.
Compute each $(O_{i} - 20)^{2}/20$.
Each category contributes $(O - E)^{2}/E$ to the Pearson statistic.
Sum to $\chi^{2}$
Reject $H_{0}$ for large $\chi^{2}$; here $2.9 < 9.488$.
2.9 < 9.488 $\Rightarrow$ do not reject $H_{0}$
$\chi^{2}$ = 2.9 on 4 df; do not reject $H_{0}$ at $\alpha$ = 0.05.
Using $\mathrm{df} = 5$ (forgetting $-1$ for the multinomial constraint) or comparing $\chi^{2}$ to a Normal $z$ critical value.
Independence uses $E_{ij} = (\text{row total} \times \text{column total})/n$ in a two-way table. That is not one-sample distributional GOF.
Two-way cross-classification; independence null; $E_{ij}=(\text{row total}\times\text{column total})/n$.
Closed-book. Two-way table: rating class $\times$ claim/no-claim. Which statement is correct?
Independence null; $E_{ij}=(\text{row total}\times\text{column total})/n$; refuse GOF conflation.

$H_{0}$: row and column classifications are independent; $E_{ij} = (\text{row i total} \times \text{column j total}) / n$. This is not the same as a chi-square GOF testing whether one sample follows a named distribution.
$H_{0}$: the counts follow a Poisson distribution with mean estimated from the table total; expected counts are that fitted Poisson pmf times n.
$H_{0}$: independence; expected counts equal the observed counts in every cell.
$H_{0}$: independence; $E_{ij}$ = row i total + column j total, without dividing by n.
Chi-square test of independence in a $2 \times 2$ fraud table

Compute all four $E_{ij} = (\text{row total} \times \text{column total})/n$.
Pearson $\chi^{2}$
Sum $(O - E)^{2}/E$ over the four cells.
Reject independence when $\chi^{2}$ exceeds the $\mathrm{df} = 1$ critical value.
$\chi^{2} = 100/21 \approx 4.762$ on 1 df; reject independence of channel and fraud flag at $\alpha = 0.05$.
Using $E_{ij} = \frac{n}{4} = 25$ (ignoring unequal margins) or forgetting to square $(O - E)$ before dividing by $E$.

Keep Type I/II in the reject-true-null / fail-to-reject-false-null directions. A p-value is a tail probability under $H_{0}$, not $P(H_{0}|\text{data})$ and not $P(H_{1})$. Power is $P(\text{reject }H_{0} \mid H_{1}\text{ true})$.
Null vs alternative; Type I = false reject; Type II = false retain; p-value = extreme-tail probability under $H_{0}$; power = $P(\text{reject} \mid H_{1})$.
Swapping Type I/II, or reading the p-value as $P(H_{0}|data)$ or $P(H_{1})$.
Closed-book. Disease screening: $H_{0}$ = no disease, $H_{1}$ = disease present. Which statement is correct?
Type I = false positive; Type II = false negative; p-value under $H_{0}$; power = $1-\beta$; concepts $\neq$ cookbook click.

Type I error is a false positive (declare disease when healthy). Type II error is a false negative (miss disease when present). A p-value is the probability under $H_{0}$ of a result at least as extreme as observed; power is $P(\text{reject }H_{0} \mid H_{1}\text{ true})$. Running a software z-test does not by itself replace this vocabulary.

A pricing team tests $H_{0}\colon \mu$ = £10,000 vs $H_{1}\colon \mu \neq$ £10,000 for mean claim cost at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$. The test statistic is $z = 2.1$ under $H_{0}$ (standard Normal). Compute the two-sided p-value and state the decision. Use $\Phi(2.1)$ = 0.9821.
$\alpha$
CMP closed. Write the two-sided p-value as $2[1 - \Phi(|z|)]$ before substituting.
Compute $1 - \Phi(2.1)$.
For a continuous symmetric null, the one-sided tail is $1 - \Phi(|z|)$.
Decision at $\alpha = 0.05$
Compare $p$ with $\alpha$.
Reject $H_{0}$ when $p \leq \alpha$. Here $p = 0.0358 < 0.05$.
$0.0358 < 0.05 \Rightarrow reject H_{0}$
Reject $H_{0}$ at 5%.
$Two-sided p-value = 0.0358$; $reject H_{0}: \mu = £10,000 at \alpha = 0.05.$
Reporting only the one-sided tail 0.0179 as the p-value for a two-sided alternative, or comparing $z$ to $\alpha$ directly ($2.1$ vs $0.05$).
You will be able to outline a permutation test from exchangeability under H₀ to a reference distribution.
Closed-book. Under $H_{0}$ of no treatment effect, treatment labels are exchangeable across units. Which statement is correct?

Shuffle or reassign labels under $H_{0}$, recompute the test statistic many times, and compare the observed statistic to that permutation reference distribution. That is not a Normal two-sample z-test by another name, and not a chi-square GOF to a named distribution.
Resample with replacement to form a percentile confidence interval; reject $H_{0}$ if zero is outside that interval, and call the procedure a permutation test.

Small claim samples (£00): Group A = {10, 12, 14}, Group B = {8, 9, 11}. Test $H_{0}$: the two groups share the same distribution, using the two-sided permutation statistic $|\bar{x}_{A} - \bar{x}_{B}|$. Enumerate all C(6,3) = 20 assignments of three labels to A. The observed $|\bar{x}_{A} - \bar{x}_{B}|$ equals 8/3. Exactly 4 of the 20 permutations have |diff| $\geq 8/3$. Report the exact permutation p-value.
permutations with $|\mathrm{diff}| \geq \text{observed}$
CMP closed. Compute the observed $|\bar{x}_{A} - \bar{x}_{B}|$, then form $p = (\#\text{ extreme})/20$.
Compute $|\mathrm{mean}(A) - \mathrm{mean}(B)|$.
Under $H_{0}$ every assignment of three labels to A is equally likely; the p-value is the proportion at least as extreme as observed.
Decision at $\alpha = 0.05$
Do not reject $H_{0}$ when $p > \alpha$.
$0.2 > 0.05 \Rightarrow$ do not reject $H_{0}$
Do not reject $H_{0}$ at 5%
Observed $|\bar{x}_{A} - \bar{x}_{B}| = 8/3$; exact permutation p-value = 0.2; do not reject $H_{0}$ at $\alpha = 0.05$.
Least squares minimises the sum of absolute residuals; the slope equals the sample correlation $\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y)$ by definition.
Least squares means clicking Fit in software; no closed-form criterion need be stated once $\hat{\beta}$ is printed.
Closed-book. Simple linear model $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x + \varepsilon$ with data pairs (xi, yi). Which statement is correct?
Minimise sum squared residuals; $\hat{\beta}_{1} = \frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}}{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}}$; refuse Fit-as-criterion and Corr-as-slope.
Accepting Fit as the criterion or $\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y)$ as the OLS slope.

Choose $\beta_{0}$, $\beta_{1}$ to minimise $\sum (y_{i} - \beta_{0} - \beta_{1} x_{i})^{2}$. Slope $\hat{\beta}_{1} = \frac{\sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})(y_{i} - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})^{2}} = \frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(X, Y)}{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X)}$; intercept $\hat{\beta}_{0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_{1} \bar{x}$. Fit implements OLS but is not the criterion; $\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y)$ is not the OLS slope.
Least squares is clicking Fit; the closed-form slope formula is optional once software returns $\hat{\beta}$.
The OLS slope equals $\operatorname{Corr}(X, Y)$ because both measure linear association on the same scale.
Minimise $\sum |y_{i} - \beta_{0} - \beta_{1} x_{i}|$; the resulting slope is $\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(X, Y)}{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X)}$ for simple linear regression.

Four (voyage risk band, cargo loss) pairs (x, y) with y in £000 are (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 7), (5, 9). Fit the simple linear model $y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$ by ordinary least squares: compute $\bar{x}$, $\bar{y}$, $S_{xx}$, $S_{xy}$, then $\hat{\beta}_{1}$ and $\hat{\beta}_{0}$. Also report the residual at x = 4.
$y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x$
CMP closed. Compute $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ first, then $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$, before forming $\hat{\beta}_{1} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$.
Compute $S_{xx} = \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})^{2}$ and $S_{xy} = \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})(y_{i} - \bar{y})$.
$S_{xx}$ measures spread in X; $S_{xy}$ measures co-movement of X and Y about their means.
$\hat{\beta}_{1} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$, $\hat{\beta}_{0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_{1} \bar{x}$, residual $= y - (\hat{\beta}_{0} + \hat{\beta}_{1} x)$.
Least squares minimises $\sum \mathrm{residual}^{2}$; the closed forms give the unique minimisers for simple linear regression.
$\hat{\beta}_{1} = 1.6$, $\hat{\beta}_{0} = 0.9$; fitted line $\hat{y} = 0.9 + 1.6x$; residual at $x = 4$ equals $-0.3$ (£000).
Using $\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}$ for the slope, or reporting the residual as $\hat{y} - y$ instead of the convention $e = y - \hat{y}$.
Today I will force the candidate to write η forms for simple and multiple LM and refuse treating 'multiple' as automatic excellence.
Closed-book. Which statement correctly writes a simple linear model for Y on X1 and a multiple linear model for Y on X1 and X2 using $\beta$ notation?
Simple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \varepsilon$. Multiple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \beta_{2} X_{2} + \varepsilon$.
Simple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \varepsilon$. Multiple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \beta_{2} X_{2} + \varepsilon$ (or equivalent $\beta$ notation).

Simple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \beta_{2} X_{2} + \varepsilon$. Multiple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \varepsilon$, because multiple means more parameters in the least-squares criterion.
Both forms are Y = $\hat{\beta}$0 + $\hat{\beta}$1 x + $\varepsilon$ where $\hat{\beta}$ comes from minimising sum of squared residuals; stating the model is the same as OLS estimation.
Simple and multiple models differ only in software menu choice; the equation $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{1} + \varepsilon$ covers both one and two predictors.
Simple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,\mathrm{age} + \varepsilon$. Multiple adds $\beta_{2}\,\mathrm{sum\_insured}$. Refuse OLS-as-form.

Simple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,\mathrm{age} + \varepsilon$. Multiple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,\mathrm{age} + \beta_{2}\,\mathrm{sum\_insured} + \varepsilon$. Writing least-squares formulae for $\hat{\beta}$ is estimation, not stating the simple versus multiple linear model forms.

Simple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,\mathrm{age} + \beta_{2}\,\mathrm{sum\_insured} + \varepsilon$. Multiple: $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,\mathrm{age} + \varepsilon$, because multiple means more parameters in the criterion.
Both forms are Y = $\hat{\beta}_{0} + \hat{\beta}_{1}$ x + $\varepsilon$ where $\hat{\beta}$ comes from minimising sum of squared residuals; stating the model is the same as clicking Fit.

Two fitted linear models for travel medical claim cost Y (£00) are available.
Simple: $\hat{Y}_{s}$ = 3.5 + 0.8$x_{1}$, where $x_{1}$ is trip length in weeks.
Multiple: $\hat{Y}_{m}$ = 2.0 + 0.6$x_{1}$ + 0.4$x_{2}$, where $x_{2}$ is a destination risk score.
For a trip with $x_{1}$ = 5 and $x_{2}$ = 3, compute both fitted values and state which model form each equation represents.
$\hat{Y}_{s}$ uses only $x_{1}$ (simple); $\hat{Y}_{m}$ uses $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ (multiple)
Substitute $x_{1} = 5$ into $\hat{Y}_{s}$.
The simple model ignores x₂ even if that covariate is available.
Substitute $x_{1} = 5$ and $x_{2} = 3$ into $\hat{Y}_{m}$.
Calling $\hat{Y}_{m}$ 'simple' because it is still linear in the parameters, or assuming the two fitted values must coincide at the same $(x_{1}, x_{2})$.
Closed-book. After fitting Y = $\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}$ x in software you see $\hat{\beta}_{1}$, SE($\hat{\beta}_{1}$), R-squared, and residual plots. For a new x-star, which statement is correct?
Mean interval for $E[Y | x*]$; prediction wider; refuse fit-only and optional residuals.

A mean-response interval covers $E[Y | x*]$; a prediction interval covers a new observation and is typically wider (adds residual variance). Fit alone is not enough: slope inference, goodness-of-fit, prediction limits, and residual checks are all required before trusting the fit.
The mean-response interval and prediction interval for x-star are the same width because both estimate $E[Y | x-star]$ only.

Software returns slope estimate $\hat{\beta}_{1} = -8$ (£ per year of pet age) with $\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{1}) = 2.5$. Treat the Normal approximation as adequate and use $z_{0.975} = 1.96$.

(b) Form the approximate 95% CI for $\beta_{1}$.

$\hat{\beta}_{1}, SE(\hat{\beta}_{1})$
CMP closed. Form z = $\hat{\beta}_{1}$/SE($\hat{\beta}_{1}$), then contrast SE_mean with SE_pred before writing intervals.
Divide $\hat{\beta}_{1}$ by its standard error.
Software inference on the slope starts from the estimate and its SE; under $H_{0}\colon \beta_{1} = 0$ the ratio is approximately standard Normal for large samples.
Approximate 95% CI for $\beta_{1}$
Compute $\hat{\beta}_{1} \pm 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{1})$.
Form $\hat{y} \pm 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}$ for each SE, and compare widths.
$z = -3.2$; 95% CI for $\beta_{1} \approx (-12.9, -3.1)$; mean interval $(290.6, 349.4)$ is narrower than individual prediction interval $(241.6, 398.4)$.

Two nested commercial-property severity regressions are fitted on the same $n = 60$ risks.
Model A uses $p = 3$ explanatory variables and has $R^{2} = 0.55$.
Model B uses $p = 6$ explanatory variables and has $R^{2} = 0.58$.

$R^{2}_{\mathrm{adj}}$ for Model A
Substitute $n = 60$, $p = 3$, $R^{2} = 0.55$ into the formula.

$R^{2}_{\mathrm{adj},A} \approx 0.5259$
$R^{2}_{\mathrm{adj}}$ for Model B

Choosing Model B solely because raw $R^{2} = 0.58$ exceeds $0.55$ without computing adjusted $R^{2}$, or assuming the larger model always loses after any penalty.
Yesterday η forms (4.2.5). Today estimation/deviance language.
Deviance 2($\ell$_sat - $\ell$_model); scaled divides by scale; MLE/IWLS. Refuse p-chopping.

Deviance compares the fitted model's log-likelihood to a saturated model (2 times $\ell$_sat minus $\ell$_model). Scaled deviance divides by dispersion or scale when relevant. Parameters are typically estimated by maximum likelihood (often via IWLS). Mechanical p-value chopping is model-choice behaviour, not deviance definition.
Deviance equals sum (y minus $\hat{\mu}$) squared; scaled deviance adds sigma hat. GLM parameters are always OLS slopes on the link scale.

A Poisson GLM fitted mean for one observation is $\hat{\mu} = 5$, and the observed count is $y = 8$. Compute the observation's deviance contribution $d = 2\bigl[y \ln(y/\hat{\mu}) - (y - \hat{\mu})\bigr]$. Then, if the total deviance across the sample is $D = 22.0$ and $\varphi = 1$, state the scaled deviance $D/\varphi$ and how parameters were estimated.
$y$, $\hat{\mu}$
$D, \phi$
CMP closed. Compute $y \ln(y/\hat{\mu})$ before doubling; then form $D/\varphi$.
Substitute y = 8 and $\hat{\mu}$ = 5 into the Poisson deviance formula.
$d \approx 1.5201$
Compute $D/\phi$.
With $\phi = 1$ the scaled deviance equals the total deviance.
$Observation deviance \approx 1.5201$; $scaled deviance = 22.0$; $parameters estimated by \mathrm{MLE} (IWLS).$
Omitting the factor of 2 in the deviance contribution, or treating $D/\phi$ as something other than scaled deviance when $\phi = 1$.
GLM responses sit in named exponential families. Package name or presence of exp() does not make a GLM. Normal is one family member, not the universal definition.
Any continuous response is automatically in the exponential family because the density can be written with an $\exp()$ somewhere.
Family membership needs the exponential-family form tied to the response structure, not software branding or exp() alone.

Example: Poisson (counts with $E[Y]=\operatorname{Var}[Y]=\mu$); binomial (bounded proportion or count responses); Normal (continuous responses with constant variance). Each has an exponential-family density usable as a GLM response. Package name is not GLM; a GLM response sits in an exponential family with later eta and link.
Poisson belongs because the pmf contains $\exp()$; that single algebraic feature is the family definition without mean-variance structure.

A policy lapse indicator is modelled as $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ with $p = 0.25$. Write the pmf in exponential-family form $\exp\{y\theta - b(\theta)\} / a(\varphi) \times c(y, \varphi)$ (with $\varphi = 1$), identify the natural parameter $\theta = \operatorname{logit}(p)$, and evaluate $\theta$ numerically. Also state why the Normal distribution is a special case within the same GLM exponential family, not a rival outside it.
CMP closed. Rewrite the pmf as $\exp\{y \operatorname{logit}(p) + \ln(1 - p)\}$ before naming θ.
$\ln \mathrm{pmf} = y \ln p + (1 - y) \ln(1 - p) = y \ln(p/(1 - p)) + \ln(1 - p)$.
$\exp\{y \ln(p/(1 - p)) + \ln(1 - p)\}$ matches $\exp\{y\theta - b(\theta)\}$ with $\theta = \operatorname{logit}(p)$
Evaluate $\theta$ at $p = 0.25$
$\theta \approx -1.0986$
Normal $\in$ exponential family (canonical link = identity)

$\theta = \operatorname{logit}(0.25) = \ln(1/3) \approx -1.0986$; Bernoulli/Binomial is exponential-family with $b(\theta) = \ln(1 + e^{\theta})$. Normal is a member of the same family, not a rival outside it.
Taking $\theta = p$ or $\theta = \ln p$ instead of $\operatorname{logit}(p)$, or claiming the Normal distribution is outside the exponential family used by GLMs.
